en: The Bhagavān Spoke the Vemacitra Sūtra, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
At that time,
a wanderer of the Vaimasura clan, having finished his midday meal, was walking about for exercise when he approached the place where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, Gautama!
Your physical form is most supreme and exquisite.
"Kātyāyana! [the Buddha replied].
"What is the excellence of form?
"Gautama, it is this:

there is form that is excellent, supremely excellent; there is nothing more excellent or more supreme than it. That form is most excellent, most beautiful; that form is the highest and most beautiful."
“It is just as if, Kaccāyana, someone were to say:
‘Among humans there is one who is exquisite; I wish to have sexual intercourse with her.’”
Or some might say this:
"Do you mean that this person who is called 'excellent' has a specific name, a specific clan, or a specific appearance?
Is he tall, short, or of medium height?"
Whether she is beautiful or not beautiful?
Whether she is fair or dark?
Whether she is the daughter of a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a craftsman?
"Is it the east, the south, the west, or the north?
Having been asked this, he was unable to reply.
"You neither know nor see, yet you claim that this person has come from the most excellent place in the north, and speak of lust."
“Kaccāyana! Regarding what you said—that ‘that form is most exquisite, that form is supreme, that form is unsurpassed’—when questioned about that form, you were unable to know it.”

"It is just as if, Gautama, Jāmbūnada gold were taken by a skilled master craftsman, polished and purified to the highest degree, and placed within a white vessel; its form and color would be most exquisite, and its luster would illuminate everything."
Therefore, Gautama, I say this:
form is the most wonderful, form is the most excellent; that form is supreme, that form is unsurpassed, that form is the highest.
"Therefore, Kaccāyana, I shall question you in return; answer as you see fit.
What do you think, Kaccāyana?"

This Jambūnada gold, when skillfully polished and refined by a master craftsman, reflects forms and colors when placed within a white vessel; that is to say, it illuminates the colors of insects even in the midst of darkness. Among all lights, which can be said to be the most excellent, supreme, wondrous, and beautiful?
“O Gautama! You have spoken of the glow-worm as having the most excellent, supreme, best, and most wonderful radiance compared to Jāmbūnada gold.
“What do you think, Kātyāyana?”
Just as the glow-worm illuminates when it is dark;
or as the light of an oil lamp illuminates when it is dark—
who’s light is most excellent, most sublime, most beautiful, and most supreme?
“Indeed, Gautama!
The light of an oil lamp illuminates the insects; that light is the most excellent, the highest, the most sublime, and the best.
“What do you think, Kātyāyana?”
That is to say, the light of an oil lamp illuminates the darkness of night;
that is to say, this great mass of fire illuminates the darkness of night with its radiance.
Which light is the most excellent, supreme, and sublime?
“Indeed, Gautama!
The radiance of a mass of fire is superior, more excellent, and most sublime compared to the light of an oil lamp.
“What do you think, Kaccāyana?”
That is to say: when a mass of fire is piled up in the darkness, its radiance illuminates;
or when the stars pass through the night, with the sky clear and free from the obscuration of clouds, their radiance illuminates.
Of these, whose radiance is most supreme, excellent, and beautiful?
“Indeed, Gautama!
The light of the stars surpasses that of a heap of fire; its radiance is most excellent, supreme, and wonderful.
“What do you think, Kātyāyana?”
That is to say: when the stars have passed the midnight hour, the sky is clear and cloudless, and their radiance shines forth;
or when it is nearly midnight on a moonlit night, the sky is cloudless, and its radiance shines forth.
Of these, whose radiance is most supreme, excellent, and beautiful?
“Indeed, Gautama!
The moon’s radiance surpasses that of the stars; its radiance is most excellent, supreme, and wonderful.
“What do you think, Kaccāyana?”
It refers to the moon at midnight on a clear night when there are no clouds to obscure it, and its radiance illuminates all;
or it refers to the sun at midday during the summer season, and its radiance illuminates all.
Of these, whose radiance is the most supreme, excellent, and beautiful?
“Indeed, Gautama!
The light of the sun is brighter than that of the moon; its radiance is the most supreme, excellent, and sublime.
“This is so, Kātyāyana!”

There are many gods who claim such majestic power and great capability that their radiance cannot reach me; they say, "I was originally seated therein, and I was originally speaking therein," yet I do not say that their radiance is supreme, that their radiance is highest, or that their radiance is most wonderful.
"Kātyāyana! Is it that you take the light of a glowworm—which is the lowest, most inferior, and least excellent—and say that it is the highest, most supreme, and most wonderful?
Having been questioned about light, you were unable to know."
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Vaimasika, having been rebuked face-to-face by the Blessed One, remained silent without a word; with his body and face soiled, he turned away and stood in silence.
Thereupon, having rebuked Vemacitra face-to-face, the Blessed One, wishing to have him speak further, addressed the heterodox ascetic Vemacitra, saying:
"Furthermore, Kātyāyana!"

There are five classes [of beings] who desire, love, and cherish forms, becoming attached through sexual passion: the eye cognizes forms, the ear cognizes sounds, the nose cognizes odors, the tongue cognizes tastes, and the body cognizes tactile sensations.

Kaccāyana, there may be forms that are pleasing and forms that are unpleasing. Suppose there is someone who is fully satisfied with a certain form; his mind is filled with joy regarding it, and he has no desire, thought, longing, acquisition-seeking, or aspiration for other forms—this is because that form is the most excellent and supreme.

Kātyāyana! There may be someone who loves sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles; or there may be someone who does not love tangibles. There may be someone for whom a certain tangible is so full of joy that their mind’s inclination is also fulfilled; toward other tangibles beyond that one, they have no desire, no thought, no wish to obtain it, and no aspiration for it—this is because that tangible is the most supreme and most exquisite.
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Vaimasura joined his palms toward the World-Honored One and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How extraordinary, Gautama!
The śramaṇa Gautama employs immeasurable skillful means to speak to me of sensual pleasure and the pursuit of sensual pleasure."
It is just as with fire, Gautama!
Grass and wood burn because of fire, and fire burns because of grass and wood.
In the same way, I am, O Śramaṇa Gautama!
"By means of immeasurable skillful means, I have spoken of sexual desire; I have spoken of the pleasure of sexual desire and the cessation of the pursuit of the pleasure of sexual desire.

Kaccāyana! It is not good for you to hold a divergent view, a divergent tolerance, a divergent inclination, and a divergent pursuit regarding this throughout this long night; you should understand the meaning of what I have said as being equal to its equal."

Kaccāyana! My disciples, the bhikkhus, constantly rise at dawn and do not sleep at evening; they always engage in discussion and discourse, and they will surely achieve the equal Way. They are fully possessed of analytical discernment; having attained birth’s end, their holy life is perfected, what was to be done has been accomplished, and they truly know that name-and-form have come to an end.
"What I have said here, you should understand its meaning as being equal to what I have stated.

Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Vairāṭīputra became extremely incensed toward the World-Honored One; harboring intense resentment and displeasure, he spoke against the World-Honored One, reviled the World-Honored One, and abused the World-Honored One, saying:
"Such is this śramaṇa Gautama!"
"It is wrong.
Having finished his reproachful speech, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This [is what you say], Gautama!"

There may be a certain śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who does not know the past world, nor does he know the future world and the immeasurable succession of births in the world; yet he makes a declaration regarding the noble one, saying: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and for name-and-form there is nothing further"—knowing this as it truly is.
Therefore, Gautama, I have this thought:

"How is it that some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, not knowing the past world and not knowing the future world—the immeasurable succession of births in the world—yet declare with noble authority: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and for name-and-form there is no further existence,' knowing this as it truly is?"
Thereupon the Blessed One thought:
"This ascetic Vairūḍaka is extremely angry with me, harbors deep resentment, and is displeased; he slanders me and reviles me."
"This ascetic Gautama!
I shall revile and speak against him," he said to me.
"O Gautama! There may be some śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who does not know the past world, yet claims to know it as it truly is.
Having understood this, the Blessed One addressed the heterodox teacher Vaimasura, saying:
"Kaccāyana! Suppose there is a certain ascetic or brahmin who, not knowing the past world, yet knows it as it truly is; at that time, he should speak thus:
'Setting aside the past world, setting aside the future world, one should not dwell upon even a single lifetime.'"
"Furthermore, Kaccāyana! I say this:
'Setting aside the past world, setting aside the future world, one should not dwell on even a single lifetime.'"

My disciples, the bhikṣus, are neither flatterers nor deceitful; they are upright in their conduct. When I instruct them and preach the Dharma to them, they are able to train according to what has been established; they draw near to the Dharma and know that there is goodness.

"It is just as, Kaccāyana, when a young boy has his hands and feet bound by his parents; at that time, consciousness arises in him. When his parents release his hands and feet, he only remembers the releasing and does not remember the binding."
"In this way, Kātyāyana,
I say: 'Setting aside the past, one comes to know that there is goodness.'"
"It is just as with Kātyāyana!

A lamp burns because of its oil and wick; if someone does not add more oil nor replace the wick, what was previously there will all be exhausted and nothing further added, so that it will soon be extinguished quickly."
"In this way, Kātyāyana!
I have spoken thus:
'Setting aside the past, one comes to know that there is goodness.'"
"It is just as, Kātyāyana,
if there were ten stacks of wood— twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty stacks of wood— and they were set ablaze and burning, one would know that there was a great mass of fire."

Suppose there is a person who no longer adds firewood, nor grass, nor cow dung, nor bran, nor sweepings; before long, everything is exhausted, and as they add nothing more, it is soon quickly extinguished.
"In this way, Kātyāyana! I speak thus:
'Setting aside the past, one comes to know that there is goodness.'"
When these words were spoken, the heterodox teacher Vimala attained the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Vimala saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and realized the purity of the Dharma; he was freed from error and doubt, no longer regarded other gods as supreme, and ceased to rely on others. Having transcended all hesitation, he established himself in the fruit and attained the state of fearlessness within the domain of the World-Honored One.
Rising from his seat, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and said:
"O World-Honored One!

May I indeed be permitted to train in the path under the World-Honored One, receive full ordination as a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the World-Honored One; this bhikṣu shall practice the holy life."
That Vimala then followed the path of training under the World-Honored One, received full ordination, and became a bhikṣu.
Having trained and received full ordination, the Venerable Vimala understood the Dharma and attained the state of an arhat.
The Buddha spoke thus.
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, Vimala rejoiced and was glad.
This is the *Vimāla-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
